Powerful quantum computers could pose a serious risk.

And preparing the world's infrastructure for quantum attacks will take longer than most people expect.

I came across this breakdown from @PaloAltoNtwks, and it got me thinking about how many systems we'd actually need to upgrade.

We're talking about:

→ Payment systems
→ Digital identities and authentication
→ Software updates and security checks
→ Older connected devices that may be difficult to update

With so much infrastructure to upgrade, I can see why NIST isn't waiting around. It finalized its first three quantum-resistant cryptography standards in 2024 and is already urging organizations to adopt them.

There's another concern, too.

Encrypted data stolen today could become readable years later, once quantum computers become powerful enough.

Lots of ground to cover, so best start early if you ask me.

Time to share a bit more about @StacysBrain – my new product that (I hope) will enter the market over the next couple of weeks.

What will it be?
MVP = an open, graded database of marketing insights and benchmarks – each with its own sample, methodology, age, and vendor interest data.

I told you about the pain (and I’m sure you know it yourself): AI often relies on outdated numbers or just hallucinates, and lots of marketing articles have zero proof or research behind them.

It’s like a circle jerk where people cross-cite each other. But once you try to find who was the first one to say something, it turns out there’s no source at all.

In some fields it’s probably fine.

In marketing, it’s a huge problem, because we invest money based on decisions that are often backed by low-quality research (or no research at all).

So I see Stacy's Brain as the fix.

We’ve been building this for the last 3 months, and the database will have 500+ insight cards (checked and vetted by my team) at release.

Very excited tbh.
Stay tuned <3

One of my more controversial bets: the AI feed will be the form factor of 2027!

Most people don’t know what to prompt, and they won’t prompt their way into complicated agentic workflows. With chat, we ask users for digital labor: figure out what AI can do, explain the task, provide the context, repeat. That’s a lot to ask if we want billions of people using agents every day. 

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.
